core.text: So far the subject has done the action: *servī dominum portant* = the slaves carry the master. Turn it round and the master becomes the subject and has it done to him: *dominus ā servīs portātur* = the master is carried by the slaves. That is **the passive (the 'is done' form)**, *genus passīvum*. Latin makes it with new endings: -tur for one (*portātur*), -ntur for several (*portantur*).

Active: *the dog bites the man*. Passive: *the man is bitten (by the dog)*. English adds *is / are* plus a participle (a verb used like an adjective); Latin changes the ending and needs no helping verb.
Replace -t with -tur and -nt with -ntur: *vocat → vocātur*, *vocant → vocantur*. Only a verb that can take an object can be passive.

invented.en: The boy is called by his mother.
The roses are picked by the girls.

core.text: *Vocat* — he calls (he is doing it). *Vocātur* — he is called (it is done to him). The -ur tail is the whole difference, and it flips who acts. The subject of a passive verb is nominative all the same: *puer vocātur*, not *puerum*.

more.text: From the learner's notes: 'voice' is the relation between the subject and the action — doing it (active) or receiving it (passive). The notes' variable vowels again: consonant stems keep them (*pōnitur, pōnuntur*; *dūcitur, dūcuntur*), a- and e-stems drop them (*aedificātur, aedificantur*; *vidētur, videntur*), i-stems drop the i in the singular but keep the u in the plural (*accipitur, accipiuntur*; *audītur, audiuntur*). Intransitive verbs — states (*est*, *dormit*), motion (*it*, *cadit*), self-contained action (*rīdet*) — have no object and so no passive; if you cannot add a sensible object, the verb cannot be passive.

Ørberg cap. VI: -tur / -ntur with *ā servō* for the doer. The other persons (-or, -ris, -mur, -minī) come later, and some passives read best as active English: *dēlectātur* = is pleased, likes; *vehitur* = rides. A&G §156, §163.
